items.stem: State what is meant by the term "double circulation".
items.answer: A system where blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a system where blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why arteries have thick, elastic walls.
items.answer: Blood leaves the heart at high pressure; thick muscle and elastic tissue withstand the pressure and stretch and recoil to smooth the flow.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Blood leaves the heart at high pressure; thick muscle and elastic tissue withstand the pressure and stretch and recoil to smooth the flow. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "Arteries always carry oxygenated blood and veins always carry deoxygenated blood." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein oxygenated blood.
items.markingKey: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein oxygenated blood. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kenji is investigating how the duration of exercise affects heart rate. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: time spent stepping on and off a step (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 min)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time spent stepping on and off a step (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 min) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: A student counts 38 pulse beats in 30 seconds. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.answer: 76 bpm
items.markingKey: M1 38 × (60 ÷ 30); A1 76 beats per minute.

items.stem:
Isabel measured the time taken for heart rate to return to resting after 2 minutes of skipping, for students who exercise different numbers of hours per week.

Exercise per week / h | Recovery time / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 318 | 305 | 318
2 | 289 | 275 | 280
4 | 225 | 221 | 226
6 | 171 | 174 | 166
8 | 115 | 114 | 113

State the exercise per week at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 2 h; range = 14 s; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 2 h; 1 range = max − min = 289 − 275 = 14 s; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Describe the path of a red blood cell from the vena cava to the aorta, naming the chambers, valves and vessels, and explain where it gains oxygen.
items.answer: Vena cava → right atrium → (tricuspid valve) → right ventricle → (semilunar valve) → pulmonary artery → capillaries of lungs: oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood → pulmonary vein → left atrium → (bicuspid valve) → left ventricle → (semilunar valve) → aorta.
items.markingKey: Vena cava → right atrium → (tricuspid valve) → right ventricle → (semilunar valve) → pulmonary artery → capillaries of lungs: oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood → pulmonary vein → left atrium → (bicuspid valve) → left ventricle → (semilunar valve) → aorta.

items.stem: "Everyone over 40 should have a free heart check every year." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Regular checks for at-risk groups are cost-effective; universal yearly checks may not be.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: early detection of high blood pressure and cholesterol; prevents costly heart attacks later. Arguments against: very expensive for health services; may cause anxiety and over-treatment. Supported judgement: Regular checks for at-risk groups are cost-effective; universal yearly checks may not be. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A blood vessel with a thick muscular, elastic wall that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure"?
items.answer: artery
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of artery.

items.stem: Explain the advantage of a double circulation.
items.answer: Blood returns to the heart after the lungs to be pumped again at high pressure, so oxygen reaches body tissues quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Blood returns to the heart after the lungs to be pumped again at high pressure, so oxygen reaches body tissues quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a vein and an artery.
items.answer: An artery carries blood away from the heart at high pressure and has a thick muscular wall and narrow lumen; a vein carries blood to the heart at low pressure, with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves.
items.markingKey: An artery carries blood away from the heart at high pressure and has a thick muscular wall and narrow lumen; a vein carries blood to the heart at low pressure, with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe Artificial pacemakers and explain what it reveals about technology and the heart.
items.answer: A small device under the skin sends electrical impulses to make the heart beat regularly when its natural pacemaker fails. Millions of people live normal lives with pacemakers, which have become smaller and longer-lasting.
items.markingKey: Context (A small device under the skin sends electrical impulses to make the heart beat regularly when its natural pacemaker fails.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Millions of people live normal lives with pacemakers, which have become smaller and longer-lasting. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to technology and the heart.

items.stem: Outline one way in which William Harvey and circulation (1628) shows evidence for circulation.
items.answer: Harvey calculated that the heart pumps far more blood each hour than the body could make from food, and showed with tourniquets that valves in veins only allow flow towards the heart. He overturned the 1400-year-old idea of Galen that blood was made and used up, showing blood circulates.
items.markingKey: Context (Harvey calculated that the heart pumps far more blood each hour than the body could make from food, and showed with tourniquets that valves in veins only allow flow towards the heart.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: He overturned the 1400-year-old idea of Galen that blood was made and used up, showing blood circulates. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evidence for circulation.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the duration of exercise affects heart rate. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Record resting heart rate with a pulse sensor; step on and off a 30 cm step at a metronome rate of 30 steps/min for 1 min; record heart rate immediately; rest until heart rate returns to resting; repeat for 2, 3 and 4 min; repeat three times; plot a line graph.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (stop if dizzy or unwell; students with heart or breathing conditions should not take part; clear the area around the step). Model: Record resting heart rate with a pulse sensor; step on and off a 30 cm step at a metronome rate of 30 steps/min for 1 min; record heart rate immediately; rest until heart rate returns to resting; repeat for 2, 3 and 4 min; repeat three times; plot a line graph.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "haemoglobin"?
options: A flap of tissue that stops blood flowing backwards
The red protein in red blood cells that combines with oxygen
A biconcave cell with no nucleus that contains haemoglobin and carries oxygen
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place
items.answer: The red protein in red blood cells that combines with oxygen
items.markingKey: B. "haemoglobin" is the red protein in red blood cells that combines with oxygen.

items.stem: Explain why a person with too few platelets bruises easily.
items.answer: Blood does not clot quickly, so small damaged vessels under the skin keep bleeding.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Blood does not clot quickly, so small damaged vessels under the skin keep bleeding. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between red blood cells and white blood cells.
items.answer: Red blood cells carry oxygen, have haemoglobin and no nucleus; white blood cells defend against pathogens, have a nucleus and are much fewer.
items.markingKey: Red blood cells carry oxygen, have haemoglobin and no nucleus; white blood cells defend against pathogens, have a nucleus and are much fewer. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A blood sample contains 4,800,000 red blood cells and 8,000 white blood cells per mm³. Calculate the ratio of red to white blood cells (to the nearest whole number) and comment.
items.answer: about 600 : 1 – red blood cells are far more numerous
items.markingKey: M1 4,800,000 ÷ 8,000; A1 ≈ 600 : 1; B1 red blood cells greatly outnumber white.

items.stem: Maya wants to find out how altitude of training camps affects the red blood cell count of athletes. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does altitude of the training camp affect red blood cell count per mm³?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (altitude of the training camp (0, 1000, 2000, 3000 m)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (red blood cell count per mm³ from a blood test after 3 weeks) in a question form.

items.stem: Rafael plans an investigation into how altitude of training camps affects the red blood cell count of athletes. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (altitude of the training camp (0, 1000, 2000, 3000 m)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which blood component is the most numerous?
items.answer: Red blood cells
items.markingKey: B. About 5 million per mm³.

items.stem: A student claims: "Blood is just red liquid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Blood is about 55% plasma (a liquid) and 45% cells and platelets.
items.markingKey: Blood is about 55% plasma (a liquid) and 45% cells and platelets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "White blood cells attack all cells in the body." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They recognise and destroy foreign cells and pathogens, not the body’s own healthy cells (except in autoimmune diseases).
items.markingKey: They recognise and destroy foreign cells and pathogens, not the body’s own healthy cells (except in autoimmune diseases). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Blood donation should be compulsory for healthy adults." Discuss.
items.answer: Donation should remain voluntary, with better campaigns to encourage it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: blood banks often run short; saves lives in surgery and accidents. Arguments against: bodily autonomy – forcing donation is unethical; religious objections; voluntary donors are more honest about health risks. items.stem: Which gas is at a higher percentage in exhaled air than inhaled air?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: Carbon dioxide. About 4% compared with 0.04%.

items.stem: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange.
items.answer: Millions of alveoli give a huge surface area; walls one cell thick give a short diffusion distance; a rich capillary network and ventilation maintain a steep concentration gradient; moist surface lets gases dissolve.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Millions of alveoli give a huge surface area; walls one cell thick give a short diffusion distance; a rich capillary network and ventilation maintain a steep concentration gradient; moist surface lets gases dissolve. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The lungs are muscles that pump air." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Lungs have no muscle of their own; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change chest volume.
items.markingKey: Lungs have no muscle of their own; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change chest volume. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Smoking bans in public places and explain what it reveals about public health evidence.
items.answer: Many countries banned smoking in enclosed public places from the 2000s; studies showed fewer hospital admissions for heart attacks and asthma afterwards. Reducing exposure to second-hand smoke had measurable health benefits within a few years.
items.markingKey: Context (Many countries banned smoking in enclosed public places from the 2000s; studies showed fewer hospital admissions for heart attacks and asthma afterwards.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Reducing exposure to second-hand smoke had measurable health benefits within a few years. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to public health evidence.

items.stem: A person takes 30 breaths per minute with 2.5 dm³ of air per breath. Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute.
items.answer: 75 dm³/min
items.markingKey: M1 breathing rate × volume per breath = 30 × 2.5; A1 75 dm³/min.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the number of minutes of exercise affects breathing rate. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Sit still for 5 min and count breaths for 1 min; jog on the spot to a metronome for 1 min; count breaths for the next minute; rest until breathing returns to normal; repeat for 2, 3 and 4 min; repeat the whole set on three days; plot a line graph.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (stop if dizzy; anyone with asthma should keep an inhaler nearby or not take part). Model: Sit still for 5 min and count breaths for 1 min; jog on the spot to a metronome for 1 min; count breaths for the next minute; rest until breathing returns to normal; repeat for 2, 3 and 4 min; repeat the whole set on three days; plot a line graph.

items.stem: "Air quality in cities is a bigger threat to lung health than smoking." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: For individuals, smoking is the bigger risk, but air pollution affects many more people, so both need action.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: affects everyone, including children, who cannot choose; linked to asthma and lung cancer. Arguments against: smoking causes far more lung cancer per person exposed. Supported judgement: For individuals, smoking is the bigger risk, but air pollution affects many more people, so both need action. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "bronchiole"?
options: A blood vessel with a thick muscular, elastic wall that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure
Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide
A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens to help draw air in
A small branching tube in the lungs leading to the alveoli
items.answer: A small branching tube in the lungs leading to the alveoli
items.markingKey: D. "bronchiole" is a small branching tube in the lungs leading to the alveoli.

items.stem: Explain the difference between inhalation and exhalation.
items.answer: In inhalation the intercostals and diaphragm contract, chest volume increases, pressure falls and air rushes in; in exhalation they relax, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is pushed out.
items.markingKey: In inhalation the intercostals and diaphragm contract, chest volume increases, pressure falls and air rushes in; in exhalation they relax, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is pushed out. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why breathing rate increases during exercise.
items.answer: Muscles respire faster and make more CO₂; breathing faster removes CO₂ and supplies more oxygen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Muscles respire faster and make more CO₂; breathing faster removes CO₂ and supplies more oxygen. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sana is investigating how the number of minutes of exercise affects breathing rate. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: duration of jogging on the spot (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 min)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: duration of jogging on the spot (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 min) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Use the bell-jar model of the lungs to explain how inhalation happens, and give one limitation of the model.
items.answer: Pulling the rubber sheet (diaphragm) down increases the volume inside the jar; pressure falls below atmospheric; air enters the balloons (lungs) through the tube (trachea), which inflate. Limitations: rigid jar does not move like ribs (no intercostal muscles); balloons are not elastic tissue with alveoli; no gas exchange shown.
items.markingKey: Pulling the rubber sheet (diaphragm) down increases the volume inside the jar; pressure falls below atmospheric; air enters the balloons (lungs) through the tube (trachea), which inflate. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fermentation"?
options: A blood cell that defends the body against pathogens
A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out into arteries
A tiny blood vessel with walls one cell thick where substances are exchanged with tissues
Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide
items.answer: Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: D. "fermentation" is anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.

items.stem: "Only animals respire." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: All living cells respire, including plants, fungi and bacteria.
items.markingKey: All living cells respire, including plants, fungi and bacteria. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration.
items.answer: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, produces CO₂ and water and releases a lot of energy; anaerobic uses no oxygen, produces lactic acid (animals) or ethanol and CO₂ (yeast) and releases much less energy.
items.markingKey: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, produces CO₂ and water and releases a lot of energy; anaerobic uses no oxygen, produces lactic acid (animals) or ethanol and CO₂ (yeast) and releases much less energy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Altitude training and Kenyan runners as an example, explain aerobic fitness.
items.answer: Many champion distance runners train at 2000+ m in Kenya and Ethiopia; their bodies adapt with more red blood cells, improving aerobic respiration at sea level. Shows how the body adapts to supply more oxygen to muscles.
items.markingKey: Context (Many champion distance runners train at 2000+ m in Kenya and Ethiopia; their bodies adapt with more red blood cells, improving aerobic respiration at sea level.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Shows how the body adapts to supply more oxygen to muscles. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to aerobic fitness.

items.stem: Yeast in sugar solution produced 24 bubbles of carbon dioxide in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate of respiration in bubbles per minute and state one reason counting bubbles is not very accurate.
items.answer: 4.8 bubbles/min; bubbles are different sizes (or some may be missed)
items.markingKey: M1 24 ÷ 5; A1 4.8 bubbles/min; B1 bubbles vary in size / hard to count – use a gas syringe.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Sports drinks containing glucose are necessary for everyone who exercises."
items.answer: Sports drinks help in long endurance events, but water is enough for most everyday exercise.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: supply glucose for respiration during long events; replace salts lost in sweat. Arguments against: most short exercise needs only water; high sugar adds unwanted energy and damages teeth. Supported judgement: Sports drinks help in long endurance events, but water is enough for most everyday exercise.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "anaerobic respiration".
items.answer: Respiration without oxygen, releasing much less energy from glucose
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: respiration without oxygen, releasing much less energy from glucose. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why muscles respire anaerobically during intense exercise.
items.answer: The heart and lungs cannot supply oxygen fast enough for the energy needed, so some glucose is respired without oxygen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The heart and lungs cannot supply oxygen fast enough for the energy needed, so some glucose is respired without oxygen. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an investigation into how the temperature affects the rate of anaerobic respiration in yeast, state the dependent variable and describe how Priya should measure it.
items.answer: volume of carbon dioxide collected in a gas syringe in 10 minutes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: volume of carbon dioxide collected in a gas syringe in 10 minutes.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ventricle"?
options: A system where blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body
The product of anaerobic respiration in animal muscles
A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out into arteries
A blood cell that defends the body against pathogens
items.answer: A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out into arteries

items.stem: What keeps the trachea open?
items.answer: Rings of cartilage

items.stem: Define the term "plasma".
items.answer: The yellow liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances such as glucose, CO₂, urea and hormones

items.stem: "Deoxygenated blood is blue." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Deoxygenated blood is dark red; veins only look blue through the skin.

items.answer: It gives a very short diffusion distance for oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide between blood and cells.

items.answer: Landsteiner found that mixing blood from different people sometimes caused clumping, and identified the A, B and O groups. Matching blood groups made blood transfusion safe and has saved millions of lives.

items.stem:
Sofia measured the concentration of lactic acid in a runner’s blood after running at different speeds on a treadmill.

Running speed / km/h | Lactic acid / mmol/dm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
8 | 1.3 | 1.4 | 1.3
10 | 2.1 | 2.1 | 2.0
12 | 3.5 | 3.4 | 3.4
14 | 5.1 | 5.4 | 5.0
16 | 7.4 | 7.8 | 7.4

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Lactic acid concentration increases with running speed, slowly at first and then much more steeply. At high speeds the muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered, so more anaerobic respiration happens, producing lactic acid.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Lactic acid concentration increases with running speed, slowly at first and then much more steeply.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At high speeds the muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered, so more anaerobic respiration happens, producing lactic acid.

items.stem:
Jonas measured the time taken for heart rate to return to resting after 2 minutes of skipping, for students who exercise different numbers of hours per week.

Exercise per week / h | Recovery time / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 287 | 267 | 279
2 | 253 | 251 | 252
4 | 205 | 203 | 209
6 | 148 | 145 | 146
8 | 104 | 98 | 98

Calculate the mean recovery time when the exercise per week was 2 h.
items.markingKey: M1 (253 + 251 + 252) ÷ 3; A1 252.0 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "The lungs are muscles that pump air." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Lungs have no muscle of their own; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change chest volume.
items.markingKey: Lungs have no muscle of their own; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change chest volume. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Lukas recorded the haemoglobin concentration of people living at different altitudes (three groups at each altitude).

Altitude / m | Haemoglobin / g/dm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 162 | 164 | 164
1000 | 160 | 172 | 170
2000 | 175 | 180 | 170
3000 | 186 | 177 | 178
4000 | 197 | 188 | 183

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The haemoglobin concentration increases with altitude. At higher altitude there is less oxygen per breath, so the body makes more haemoglobin to carry enough oxygen to the tissues.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The haemoglobin concentration increases with altitude.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At higher altitude there is less oxygen per breath, so the body makes more haemoglobin to carry enough oxygen to the tissues.

items.stem: Briefly describe Altitude training and Kenyan runners and explain what it reveals about aerobic fitness.
items.answer: Many champion distance runners train at 2000+ m in Kenya and Ethiopia; their bodies adapt with more red blood cells, improving aerobic respiration at sea level. Shows how the body adapts to supply more oxygen to muscles.
items.markingKey: Context (Many champion distance runners train at 2000+ m in Kenya and Ethiopia; their bodies adapt with more red blood cells, improving aerobic respiration at sea level.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Shows how the body adapts to supply more oxygen to muscles. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to aerobic fitness.

items.stem: Rafael investigated how the duration of exercise affects heart rate. The method had this weakness: pulse was counted by hand for 6 s and multiplied by 10. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use a pulse sensor or count for 30 s and double, to reduce counting errors
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use a pulse sensor or count for 30 s and double, to reduce counting errors

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the number of minutes of exercise affects breathing rate. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): stop if dizzy; anyone with asthma should keep an inhaler nearby or not take part. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. stop if dizzy; anyone with asthma should keep an inhaler nearby or not take part); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Describe the four components of blood and explain how each is adapted to its function.
items.answer: Red blood cells: haemoglobin, no nucleus, biconcave – carry oxygen. White blood cells: phagocytes engulf pathogens (flexible membrane, enzymes), lymphocytes make antibodies. Platelets: fragments that release chemicals to form a clot (fibrin) – seal wounds. Plasma: liquid carrying dissolved glucose, amino acids, CO₂, urea, hormones and heat.
items.markingKey: Red blood cells: haemoglobin, no nucleus, biconcave – carry oxygen. White blood cells: phagocytes engulf pathogens (flexible membrane, enzymes), lymphocytes make antibodies. Platelets: fragments that release chemicals to form a clot (fibrin) – seal wounds. Plasma: liquid carrying dissolved glucose, amino acids, CO₂, urea, hormones and heat.

items.stem: Compare what happens in a sprinter’s leg muscles during a 100 m race with what happens during a slow 5 km jog, using ideas about respiration.
items.answer: Sprint: energy demand exceeds oxygen supply, so much anaerobic respiration: glucose → lactic acid, little energy per glucose; lactic acid builds up → fatigue; oxygen debt repaid after (heavy breathing). Jog: heart and lungs supply enough oxygen; aerobic respiration in mitochondria: glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water, much more energy per glucose; can continue for a long time.
items.markingKey: Sprint: energy demand exceeds oxygen supply, so much anaerobic respiration: glucose → lactic acid, little energy per glucose; lactic acid builds up → fatigue; oxygen debt repaid after (heavy breathing). Jog: heart and lungs supply enough oxygen; aerobic respiration in mitochondria: glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water, much more energy per glucose; can continue for a long time.

items.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right?
options: It pumps blood all around the body at higher pressure
items.answer: It pumps blood all around the body at higher pressure
items.markingKey: D. The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

items.stem: Define the term "alveoli".
items.answer: Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The yellow liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances such as glucose, CO₂, urea and hormones"?
items.answer: plasma
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of plasma.

items.stem: Explain why bread dough rises when left in a warm place.
items.answer: Yeast respires anaerobically, producing carbon dioxide bubbles that are trapped in the dough; warmth speeds up the enzymes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Yeast respires anaerobically, producing carbon dioxide bubbles that are trapped in the dough; warmth speeds up the enzymes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a vein and an artery.
items.answer: An artery carries blood away from the heart at high pressure and has a thick muscular wall and narrow lumen; a vein carries blood to the heart at low pressure, with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves.
items.markingKey: An artery carries blood away from the heart at high pressure and has a thick muscular wall and narrow lumen; a vein carries blood to the heart at low pressure, with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between exhalation and inhalation.
items.answer: In inhalation the intercostals and diaphragm contract, chest volume increases, pressure falls and air rushes in; in exhalation they relax, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is pushed out.
items.markingKey: In inhalation the intercostals and diaphragm contract, chest volume increases, pressure falls and air rushes in; in exhalation they relax, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is pushed out. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how phagocytes protect the body.
items.answer: They move to infected areas, engulf pathogens and digest them with enzymes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They move to infected areas, engulf pathogens and digest them with enzymes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between respiration and photosynthesis.
items.answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen in all living cells; photosynthesis uses light to make glucose and oxygen from CO₂ and water in green plants.
items.markingKey: Respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen in all living cells; photosynthesis uses light to make glucose and oxygen from CO₂ and water in green plants. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and exhaled air contains 17% oxygen. A person breathes 10 dm³ of air per minute. Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed into the blood each minute.
items.answer: 0.4 dm³
items.markingKey: M1 difference = 4%; M1 10 × 4 ÷ 100; A1 0.4 dm³.

items.stem: A blood sample contains 5,200,000 red blood cells and 7,500 white blood cells per mm³. Calculate the ratio of red to white blood cells (to the nearest whole number) and comment.
items.answer: about 693 : 1 – red blood cells are far more numerous
items.markingKey: M1 5,200,000 ÷ 7,500; A1 ≈ 693 : 1; B1 red blood cells greatly outnumber white.

items.stem: Ana is investigating how the temperature affects the rate of anaerobic respiration in yeast. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If temperature increases up to about 35 °C, then more CO₂ will be produced, because enzymes in yeast work faster; above 45 °C the rate will fall because enzymes denature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If temperature increases up to about 35 °C, then more CO₂ will be produced, because enzymes in yeast work faster; above 45 °C the rate will fall because enzymes denature.

items.stem: A heart pumps 6.5 dm³ of blood per minute, with 100 cm³ per beat. Calculate the heart rate.
items.answer: 65 beats per minute
items.markingKey: M1 convert 6.5 dm³ = 6500 cm³; M1 heart rate = 6500 ÷ 100; A1 65 bpm.

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and exhaled air contains 16% oxygen. A person breathes 6 dm³ of air per minute. Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed into the blood each minute.
items.answer: 0.3 dm³
items.markingKey: M1 difference = 5%; M1 6 × 5 ÷ 100; A1 0.3 dm³.

items.stem: An adult has 5.5 dm³ of blood, of which 55% is plasma. Calculate the volume of plasma in dm³.
items.answer: 3.02 dm³

items.stem: Yeast in sugar solution produced 15 bubbles of carbon dioxide in 2 minutes. Calculate the rate of respiration in bubbles per minute and state one reason counting bubbles is not very accurate.
items.answer: 7.5 bubbles/min; bubbles are different sizes (or some may be missed)
items.markingKey: M1 15 ÷ 2; A1 7.5 bubbles/min; B1 bubbles vary in size / hard to count – use a gas syringe.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Everyone over 40 should have a free heart check every year."
items.answer: Regular checks for at-risk groups are cost-effective; universal yearly checks may not be.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: early detection of high blood pressure and cholesterol; prevents costly heart attacks later. Arguments against: very expensive for health services; may cause anxiety and over-treatment. Supported judgement: Regular checks for at-risk groups are cost-effective; universal yearly checks may not be.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "E-cigarettes should be banned for everyone because they are unsafe."
items.answer: They should be strictly controlled for young people, but may reduce harm for adult smokers trying to quit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: contain addictive nicotine; long-term effects are not fully known; flavours attract young people. Arguments against: far fewer harmful chemicals than tobacco smoke; help adult smokers quit. Supported judgement: They should be strictly controlled for young people, but may reduce harm for adult smokers trying to quit. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Blood donation should be compulsory for healthy adults." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Donation should remain voluntary, with better campaigns to encourage it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: blood banks often run short; saves lives in surgery and accidents. Arguments against: bodily autonomy – forcing donation is unethical; religious objections; voluntary donors are more honest about health risks. Supported judgement: Donation should remain voluntary, with better campaigns to encourage it. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the temperature affects the rate of anaerobic respiration in yeast. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Mix 1 g yeast with 25 cm³ 5% glucose solution in a boiling tube; cover with a layer of oil; connect to a gas syringe; place in a water bath at 20 °C for 5 min; record the gas volume after 10 min; repeat at 30, 40, 50 °C; repeat three times.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (take care with hot water; wash hands after handling yeast). Model: Mix 1 g yeast with 25 cm³ 5% glucose solution in a boiling tube; cover with a layer of oil; connect to a gas syringe; place in a water bath at 20 °C for 5 min; record the gas volume after 10 min; repeat at 30, 40, 50 °C; repeat three times.
